The map's label, in its 1945 snapshot, for Portuguese Guinea, Portugal's small colony on the West African coast, now Guinea-Bissau.

Portuguese traders had bought slaves on these rivers since the 1500s, from posts such as Cacheu and Bissau, linked to the islands of Cape Verde. The colony was separated from Cape Verde in 1879, but Portugal controlled the interior only after long campaigns that ended in the 1930s. In 1941 the capital moved from Bolama to Bissau.

Under the dictatorship of Salazar the colony was poor and had almost no schools. In 1956 Amilcar Cabral founded the PAIGC, which began an armed struggle in 1963 and soon held much of the country. Cabral was murdered in 1973, months before the party declared independence. Portugal recognised it in 1974, after the Carnation Revolution.
